text: I started this as a follow-up to the pelican-on-a-bicycle test, pushed toward inter-object physics. Every time a new model drops, I ask it for a single HTML file of a rainbow slinky walking down an up escalator forever, with real physics instead of a scripted animation. Fifteen models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have tried it so far. It’s a silly test, though it’s turned into a surprisingly good gut-check for how capable these models actually are. Getting a slinky to flip down moving steps without stalling or flying off takes spring physics, step collisions and enough self-testing to spot when the result looks off. Each model gets this exact prompt once in an empty folder, with no follow-ups or manual edits. I set reasoning effort to xhigh, or high when the agent doesn’t offer xhigh. Make a single HTML file of a rainbow slinky walking down an up escalator, in perpetual motion. Make it realistic and not a scripted animation. Rules - One fresh, empty folder per model. - Reasoning effort xhigh, or high where the agent doesn't offer xhigh. - Send the prompt once. No follow-ups and no edits to the output. - Build time runs from sending the prompt to the agent's final answer. Agents as run - Codex CLI 0.167.0 and 0.169.1: model_reasoning_effort = "xhigh" - Claude Code 2.1.322: /effort xhigh - Antigravity CLI 1.5.10: --effort xhigh, or high where xhigh is not offered Recording - Chromium at 1280 x 720 with 2x to 3x pixel density. - A fixed 60 Hz virtual clock drives requestAnimationFrame and performance.now. - Press Start, let it run 0.2 s, then capture 20 s, cropped to the slinky. Even with “not a scripted animation” in the prompt, several models still bend the rules to keep the slinky going. A few adjust the escalator speed to hold it in frame. Others add a small torque assist or reset the slinky if it stalls. These are single runs across three different agents (Codex CLI, Claude Code and Antigravity CLI), recorded on a virtual 60 Hz clock so heavy sims don’t drop frames. It’s purely an anecdotal check. Build time runs from sending the prompt to the agent’s final answer, including any self-testing the agent did along the way. API cost is what each run’s tokens would have cost at that day’s API prices, though I ran all of these on subscription plans. The first version of this test ran on Sep 4, 2026 with a different prompt.
